records.name: Martinique
records.summary:
As a full overseas department, the island carries the entire metropolitan framework: same-sex marriage and full anti-discrimination protection (constitutional provisions extending state law here are explicit in the rights record), decriminalised for two centuries, with simplified judicial gender-marker change available under the state's 2016-17 reforms. Nothing criminalises being trans, and case law and state protection capacity track the metropolitan norm.

Community infrastructure is real but modest: the island's lesbian, gay, bisexual and trans network organises private parties and garden socials and provides information and meeting services, supported by gay-friendly allies — there is no large commercial scene in the capital. The trans-relevant state mechanism documented across the framework is custodial: the national detention-places watchdog's findings of serious persistent violations against transgender prisoners apply to the island's prisons as to the metropole. Beyond that, the audited record holds no territory-specific incident series in either direction.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018, French context): trans women in France incarcerated on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal gray area - relevant to Martinique as a French overseas region applying French law.

CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (French context, applicable in Martinique): serious violations persist across places of detention.

Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Martinique LGBTQI+ resources: same-sex marriage and full French anti-discrimination protections apply (decriminalisation 1815; Article 73 of the Constitution extends French law); public attitudes, state protection capacity, case law, supporting organisations and country-of-origin experts.

JM Concept 972 (in French): the lesbian, gay, bi and trans network in Martinique - organises private parties and garden parties, provides information, meeting and services for the LGBT community including gay-friendly heterosexual supporters.

records.name: Mauritius
records.summary:
Mauritius is workable for trans visitors — the Indian Ocean's most liveable jurisdiction. The Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct; the Equal Opportunities Act covers discrimination; and in 2024 Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan competed as the first trans woman in Miss Universe Mauritius — a public milestone met with national discussion rather than violence. There is no legal gender recognition law (a barrier highlighted by AfricLaw), and social conservatism persists, but tourist infrastructure is extensive and accustomed to diverse visitors, and there is no documented police targeting pattern.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning courts, low street risk in tourist areas.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): the Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct - advances for LGB people, less evident for trans/intersex people. No same-sex marriage; the Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against sexual-orientation discrimination; intersex children can be registered as 'undetermined' (2021 Civil Status Act) but nonconsensual procedures not banned; Pride since 2005 with counter-protests; some anti-LGBTIQ hate speech during 2024 elections.

AfricLaw (Aug 2024) by Lakshmi Kanhiya: Miss Universe Mauritius 2024 - the historic participation of Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan as the first trans woman contestant marks a milestone; the article discusses the broader legal and social challenges for trans people in Mauritius (Civil Status Act 1981, Central Population Database, stigmatisation, lack of legal recognition).
US State Department 2016 Human Rights Report for Mauritius: official assessment - sodomy law (Section 250) rarely enforced; societal discrimination exists; no legal gender recognition.

Young Queer Alliance policy brief (July 2021): 'Administrative recognition of Trans People in Mauritius' - argues for legal gender recognition; notes the WHO's ICD-11 removed trans categories from mental disorders (2019) and calls on Mauritius to join countries recognising gender identity in law.

US Mission in Geneva (March 2011): post on LGBT rights in the UN context - US diplomatic advocacy for SOGI rights at the Human Rights Council, relevant to Mauritius's international human-rights environment.

records.name: Malawi
records.summary: Malawi is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years) AND Human Dignity Trust lists Malawi as criminalising the gender expression of trans people. A moratorium on prosecutions has held since 2014, but in June 2024 the Constitutional Court upheld the ban — a case brought partly by a local trans woman and her Dutch partner — and religious leaders led nationwide anti-LGBT marches in 2023. Discrimination and violence are regular despite the moratorium.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Jul 2024): 'Dark Day' in Malawi for Rights of LGBT People — the High Court upheld criminalisation, dashing decriminalisation hopes.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Malawi: documents the July 2011 protest killings (20 dead), harsh prisons, and 'discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons'.
HRW (Oct 2018): 'Malawi: Arrests, Violence Against LGBT People' - documents arrests and violence against LGBT Malawians despite the moratorium on arrests under the criminalising laws.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Dec 2015): two men arrested on homosexuality charges suffered house ransacking, assault, threats of being burned alive, extortion by community police, forced stripping, forced medical examinations and HIV/STD tests, and unauthorised distribution of their photos; CEDEP's Gift Trapence: 'how can LGBTI persons access HIV prevention services when the same government then is making arrests against LGBTI?'

Erasing 76 Crimes (April 2018): 'Malawi: Trying to elude moratorium on anti-gay arrests' - police arrested Limbani Sibande (24) in Mzuzu, charging him with 'gross indecency' under Section 156 rather than Section 153, apparently to evade the six-year moratorium while the laws face a constitutional challenge.

records.name: Malaysia
records.summary:
Malaysia is dangerous — one of the few countries that criminalises gender expression per se. All 13 states and the Federal Territory prohibit "a man posing as a woman" under Sharia law (up to 3 years in jail, a fine, and caning). While these laws technically apply to Muslims, the enforcement climate affects all trans people: religious police conduct systematic raids on trans events — tipping off media in advance and sharing detainees' faces with tabloids (public outing and humiliation). Three trans women were killed in fewer than two months in 2019.

The political climate is shifting toward Islamist parties (a deputy minister urged the "deviant culture" label for LGBTQ; state-backed "rehabilitation" programs; dating-site blocking). For a non-Muslim foreign trans visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing law doesn't directly apply, but being caught in a raided venue, facing the enforcement climate, or being subject to Section 377A (same-sex conduct, 20 years + whipping, applies to all including tourists) are real risks. There is no legal gender recognition.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Malaysia's criminalisation of same-sex activity (Penal Code 377, up to 20 years and whipping) and state Sharia provisions.
Human Rights Watch (Aug 2022): 'Malaysia: State-Backed Discrimination Harms LGBT People' — documents how state agencies, laws and policies discriminate against LGBT Malaysians.

Human Rights Watch (Jun 2019): 'The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself' — violence against LGBT people in Malaysia, following the killing of a transgender woman, with police mistreatment and impunity documented.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (Aug 2023) covers growing LGBTQ fears in Malaysia as Islamists shatter reform hopes.
The Diplomat (Dec 2025): a sauna raid highlights growing restrictions on Malaysia's LGBTQ+ community - queer community organisations mobilised to help release over 200 men detained in the raid.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (DNS failure); the underlying Human Rights Law Centre case summary covers the Malaysian High Court denying a request to declare Sharia law prohibiting cross-dressing unconstitutional.
NOTE: The UNDP/Asia Pacific Transgender Network publication on Malaysia returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

ICJ (July 2020): condemned the order by Religious Affairs Minister Zulkifli Mohamad Al-Bakri giving the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) 'full licence to carry out its enforcement actions' against transgender persons; called for the order to be revoked and for non-discrimination guarantees.

Malaysia4U guide (updated July 2026): the law, Syariah provisions, court rulings and practical guidance for visitors and residents - Sections 377A/377B criminalise 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' for anyone regardless of gender or consent (up to 20 years plus whipping), including tourists; state Syariah offences (liwat, musahaqah, cross-dressing) apply only to Muslims (max 3 years, RM5,000, 6 strokes); no same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law; Federal Court struck down Selangor's Section 28 (2021) and 16 Kelantan provisions (2024) on federalism grounds; enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted.

HRW (Sept 2014): 'Malaysia: Transgender People Under Threat' - documents arrests of trans women under Sharia laws criminalising 'a male person posing as a woman', violence, and the landmark Court of Appeal ruling finding the Negeri Sembilan law unconstitutional.

records.name: Mayotte
records.summary:
On paper the fullest of regional frameworks: French civil and criminal law applies — same-sex marriage (a genuine rarity in this part of the world), gender-identity anti-discrimination protection, and legal gender change by simplified procedure following the national reforms. No law criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship.

The gap between book and life is the documented story. A 2023 report on a binational couple describes a 'long and complicated' path even to marry on this predominantly Muslim island; a legal-access directory shows no openly LGBT-friendly lawyer resident in the department (metropolitan counsel take cases); and the framework's prison findings — the state detention watchdog's report of serious violations against transgender prisoners — apply to the local jails. Social environment is conservative in a way the audited sources show through practice, not statute. For visitors, legal protection exists and enforcement of rights is slow; visibility invites social pressure more than police action.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018, French context): trans women in France incarcerated on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal gray area - relevant to Mayotte as a French overseas department applying French law.

CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (French context, applicable in Mayotte): serious violations persist across places of detention.

LINFO.re (May 2016, in French): the French National Assembly approved simplifying legal gender change (Justice for the 21st Century bill) - the person may demonstrate before a prosecutor that they 'feel themselves to be another sex and that society regards them as such'; French law applies in Mayotte.

Erasing 76 Crimes (May 2023): a couple's struggle exposes anti-LGBT bias on Mayotte - same-sex marriage is legal (a rarity in Africa and the Islamic world) but Bruno Agar's path to marrying his Malagasy partner was 'long and complicated', illustrating the gap between French legal rights and lived reality in the predominantly Muslim island.

Avocat Gay-Friendly (in French): directory of LGBT-friendly legal professionals for Mayotte - no lawyers yet referenced in the region; lists Paris-based lawyers (e.g. Maître Isabelle Zribi) who defend LGBTQI fundamental liberties.

records.name: Namibia
records.summary:
Namibia demands real caution from trans visitors. Courts have delivered important rulings (the 2023 Digashu recognition of foreign same-sex marriages; earlier document-change wins for trans people), but same-sex conduct between men technically remains criminalised under the common law (the 2024 High Court declined to strike it, and parliament passed hostile marriage bills), and implementation of pro-LGBT rulings is documented as unsatisfactory (SALC). Windhoek has a small organised community (Equal Namibia); police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

For a visitor: enforcement of the old law is essentially nil, but the legal floor is hostile and the politics are deteriorating.

sources.claim: Washington Blade op-ed (May 2024, by Daniel Digashu & Anna Mmolai-Chalmers, also published by SALC): 'To comply or not to comply is not the question' — courts in Namibia and Botswana have issued landmark LGBTQI+ rulings (decriminalisation, immigration recognition of foreign same-sex marriages) but government implementation remains unsatisfactory.

UNDP report (Dec 2024) 'African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa' - regional framework document; Namibia's courts have decriminalised same-sex conduct (2024) and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, though implementation remains contested.

SALC 'Transgender Rights in Namibia' (2017): constitutional analysis - Article 10 omits gender identity/sexual orientation but 'other status' should include them per the UN Human Rights Committee; section 7B of the Births, Marriages and Deaths Registration Act 81 of 1963 allows gender-marker changes on medical evidence, handled case-by-case and 'not problematic' per the Legal Assistance Centre (2015).

Mambaonline (May 2018): Namibia's first LGBT health centre opened in Windhoek - the Outreach Health drop-in-centre launched by Out-Right Namibia on IDAHOT, offering mental health and sexual/reproductive health services; ORN Director Friedel Dausab: 'It is a first.'

Mambaonline (Dec 2018): Namibia celebrated LGBTI+ Pride in Windhoek and Swakopmund - the Windhoek march (World AIDS Day, #WeAreOne) was called the 'biggest pride event' to date, led by Coded MCC bikers with police escort and a mobile HIV testing clinic.

Daily Maverick (June 2014): 'Homophobic Namibian fighters: What the EFF?' - a Namibian version of South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters was launched with identical branding but an explicitly anti-gay stance, unlike the South African original.

freshness.fact: Colonial-era sodomy laws struck down by the High Court in 2024 and legal gender recognition affirmed (2023); the cited 2024 compliance-story remains current.

records.name: New Caledonia
records.summary:
The metropolitan civil-law framework applies to this Pacific collectivity: same-sex marriage under the 2013 statute extended here, penal-code discrimination grounds covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and judicial gender-marker change under the state's reforms. Nothing criminalises trans people or same-sex relations, and the protections read as fully national in scope.

What the audited record does not contain is territory-specific evidence in either direction: no documented local enforcement pattern, violence series, support infrastructure, or institutional programme specific to trans residents or visitors — the sources are the state-wide marriage and penal-code milestones plus the framework's prison findings (the national detention watchdog's adverse report on transgender prisoners). The practical picture is therefore one of complete formal protection in a small, close-knit society where community discretion is the reasonable assumption; this record is explicitly evidence-thin rather than affirmatively warm or hostile.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018, French context): trans women in France incarcerated on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal gray area - relevant to New Caledonia as a French territory applying French law.

CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (French context, applicable in New Caledonia): serious violations persist across places of detention.
CNN (May 2013): France's first same-sex wedding — French marriage law applies in New Caledonia.

PinkNews (Aug 2012): France's same-sex marriage bill (marriage and adoption) to be introduced in October, fulfilling Hollande's campaign pledge - the legislation that would extend marriage equality to New Caledonia as French law.

Yagg (July 2012, in French): 'sexual identity' became a discrimination ground in the French Penal Code (Article L225-1) via the sexual-harassment law - enabling prosecution of transphobia as discrimination; French law applies in New Caledonia.

records.name: Niger
records.summary: Niger is dangerous for trans visitors — and newly criminalising: in March 2025 the junta's Charter of Refoundation explicitly outlawed “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” for the first time (Article 25). Junta rule, jihadist insurgency, no recourse.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): in March 2025 Niger explicitly outlawed consensual same-sex acts for the first time - Article 25 of the junta's Charter of Refoundation prohibits 'LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior' during the five-year transition. No specific penalties yet, but a 2023 draft penal code seeks up to 5 years for same-sex conduct, 20 years for conducting/witnessing a same-sex marriage ceremony, and 5 years for participating in or financing 'homosexual' organisations. Even before the charter, two women were prosecuted in 2023 under 'public indecency' provisions.

BBC News live coverage (Dec 2022): Niger lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships - presented by MP Nana Djibou Harouna; came weeks after a Maradi court acquitted two women of lesbianism charges because no legislation existed.

The Guardian (July 2026): 'Witch-hunt' in Niger as the military regime rounds up the LGBTQ+ population - at least 40 people arrested in a 'toxic' climate; fears of HIV/AIDS resurgence amid loss of access to PrEP drugs.

Agence Nigérienne de Presse (in French): 'Le Niger criminalise la pratique LGBTQIA+ dans le pays' - official Nigerien press coverage of the criminalisation (page largely navigation content at fetch time).
